statement: A path-limited `git commit -- <pathspec>` over a staged rename (delete-old, add-new) silently drops the deletion if the old path is not itself named in the pathspec: the new path's content lands, but the old path is carried forward unchanged from the parent commit, and its staged deletion is left pending in the index for a later commit to pick up by accident or not at all. The commit succeeds with no error, so nothing signals the omission at commit time. Re-running the downstream check that cares about the old path being gone (here, a measurement-freeze guard diffing against a base revision) is what caught it — the guard still refused, listing the file that was supposedly moved away, because it still existed in HEAD. When committing a rename with an explicit pathspec (required here since `git add -A`/`git commit -am` are disallowed), name both the old and new paths, and re-verify against the downstream check rather than trusting a clean commit.

movesWhen.reason: This is a recurring Git invocation practice, not a missing code fix: name both old and new paths when committing a staged rename with an explicit pathspec, then verify the resulting tree with the downstream guard. No corrective implementation commit can enforce every future invocation.
